newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to try leading Socialists for corruption.
newsitem.headline: Spain to try leading Socialists for corruption.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court has decided to charge senior officials of the former ruling Socialist party with illegal party funding, court documents published on Friday showed.

Guillermo Galeote, former finance director for the Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), and its former accounts director Aida Alvarez, were among 26 people to be charged in the Filesa corruption case, the documents showed.
Seven people including two former Socialist parliamentarians have already been accused in the Filesa case, named after a front-company set up to channel funds to the party.
The court moved the case closer to the Socialist leadership by charging a further 19 people, including the ex-finance directors.
But it decided not to try any bankers or financiers whom the state prosecutor had accused of trying to buy government favour.
Left-wing opposition spokeswoman Rosa Aguilar called on former prime minister and PSOE secretary general Felipe Gonzalez to accept political responsibility for the scandal and resign.

"It seems ever clearer and necessary that Felipe Gonzalez should end his silence, show his face and speak, because he has those responsible for his party's finances, men and women of his confidence, embroiled in a court case," she told journalists.
"He should clarify the presumed party financing and assume the judicial and political responsibilities for it."

The state prosecutor said 10 Spanish companies paid more than 1.08 billion pesetas ($8.3 million) to several front companies, set up by those who are to stand trial, for bogus studies and reports. In return they received government favours.

The companies included Spanish banks Banco Bilbao Vizcaya and the former Banco Central, private oil company Espanola de Petroleos SA-Cepsa, bus and truck company Empresa Nacional de Autocamiones-ENASA, supermarket chain Centros Comerciales Pryca and construction company Fomento de Obras and Construcciones SA.

The front companies -- Malesa, Time Export and Filesa -- were used to fund Socialist party election campaigns starting in 1989 with a general election and a European parliament poll, according to the state prosecutor.

The scandal came to light more than three years ago and embarrassed the former Socialist government, which was already reeling from charges it ran a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels and charges it bugged leading society figures.
It contributed to the party's election defeat in March after 13 years in power.
State investigators were unable to establish that the party's executive body had agreed to the Filesa scheme.
After learning about the court decision, Socialist party spokesman Cipria Ciscar said the party respected the judicial process and asked for a speedy resolution.
"We are asking for swiftness in its judicial resolution," Ciscar said in a statement. "The PSOE has always had respect for judicial decisions, in this case as in all." ($1=130 pesetas)
